control_ladder.note_beginner: If you are still choosing what to plant, look at how the variety carries its fruit. Some elderberries, Bob Gordon among them, flip their berry clusters downward once the fruit has set, which tucks the berries into the foliage, and those plantings tend to lose fewer of them to birds.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivars with inverting cymes, Bob Gordon the named example here, present ripening fruit downward and inside the canopy rather than held up on top of it, with lower reported bird loss as a result. It is a decision made at planting, so weigh it when a new shrub goes in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick each cluster as soon as it is ready and clear the bush as you work through it, rather than leaving ripe fruit hanging for another week. Anything still up there is what the birds are working on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ripe fruit left on the shrub is the standing invitation, so a tight picking interval shortens the window in which there is anything worth raiding. Birds are widely the leading competitor for this crop and a flock can take most of it within a few days of the fruit blackening, which is what puts weight on picking on time.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shiny tape, spinning reflectors and plastic owls will push birds off a bush at first. The catch is that they get used to them, and after that the devices stop earning their keep. Use them to buy a little time, and plan on netting for the fruit you want to keep.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Visual and noise devices give brief relief before habituation sets in, so on a crop birds rank this highly they support the netting rather than stand in for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the step that actually holds. Drape bird netting over the shrub, or over a frame built around it, before the berries begin to darken, and tuck or pin the edges in at the base so nothing can get underneath. Putting it up after the birds have found the fruit is too late to help much.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Netting over the shrub or carried on a frame, with the skirt secured at ground level, is the dependable control. Install ahead of coloring rather than at first damage, and seal the base, since an open skirt simply routes the birds under the mesh.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick ripe clusters often, and strip the whole cluster instead of taking the easy berries, so nothing soft is left hanging. Get what you pick into the refrigerator soon after, since the fly lays its eggs in good ripe fruit and the beetles arrive on anything that has gone over. A tight picking schedule is the main tool you have here.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Frequent, clean harvest works on both halves of this problem: spotted wing drosophila lays into sound ripe fruit, so the picking interval sets how much susceptible fruit is standing at any moment, while sap beetles arrive on whatever is allowed to go overripe or split. Cool the picked fruit promptly rather than letting it sit warm.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear up berries that have dropped and clusters that have gone soft or split, and bag them for the trash rather than the compost pile. Overripe fruit on the ground and on the bush is what draws the beetles in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitation is the other half of the same program: overripe and split fruit is what sap beetles are drawn to, and culls left lying keep a food source sitting under the planting. Bag what you pull rather than composting it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A cup of apple cider vinegar hung near the fruit catches the flies and tells you they have arrived, so you know when the picking and cleanup really matter. It is a warning device, not a control: the trap will not bring the numbers on the bush down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cider vinegar traps report the fly's presence and let you tighten the harvest interval on evidence rather than on guesswork. Detection only, since trap catch is not population reduction.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When a cane, meaning one of the shrub's main stems, wilts or dies back and you find it hollow and tunneled, cut it out below the damage and get rid of it straight away, because the grub is inside the piece you just took off. Do the same each winter with old and damaged canes, and carry the trimmings away from the bush instead of leaving them in a pile nearby.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removal is the control here. The larvae feed inside the cane, so cutting an infested or wilting cane out below the tunneling and destroying it takes the insect with the wood; nothing applied to the outside reaches them. Annual dormant renewal of old and damaged canes is the preventive half, and it holds only if the prunings leave the site rather than overwintering in a pile beside the planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. A heavy push of nitrogen gives the shrub a flush of soft new shoots, and soft new shoots are what aphid colonies build up on. Look over the new growth in spring while you are out there, since that is where they show up first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained feeding keeps the shrub from throwing the flush of tender shoot tips colonies establish on. Pair it with a scouting habit on new spring growth, which is where the first colonies and the first curled tips appear.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a light patch, knock them off with a hose. Aphids are soft and most of the ones you dislodge do not get back up. Do it earlier in the day so the leaves have time to dry off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful jet dislodges colonies from a woody shrub that can take the pressure, and it costs you none of the predators already working the same shoots, which a spray would. Time it early enough that foliage dries.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids and will usually handle a light infestation for you. Supporting them mostly means leaving them alone: skip the broad, kill-everything sprays that take them out along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident predators, ladybugs prominent among them, are the standing suppression on an established elderberry and generally hold light colonies without help. Conserving them means keeping broad-spectrum material out of the canopy, which is the argument for the feeding and water steps coming first.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a colony gets away from you, insecticidal soap kills the aphids you actually wet, so cover the shoot tips and the undersides of leaves where they are sitting. It only works while it is wet, so you may need to repeat it, and skip it on a plant that is dry and stressed or during hot weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Contact material with no residual: coverage of shoot tips and leaf undersides decides the outcome, and repeat applications are the norm. It also kills the soft-bodied beneficials it wets directly, so spot-treat the colonies rather than washing the whole shrub, and hold off on stressed plants and in heat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go out in the cool of the morning while the beetles are still slow and knock them into a tub of soapy water. That is usually all a healthy elderberry asks for, since a strong shrub grows past a fair bit of chewed foliage. Skip the lure traps sold for these beetles, because they pull more in than they take out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Morning handpicking into soapy water, while the adults are sluggish, is the practical control. A vigorous established shrub usually grows past a fair amount of skeletonized leaf, so light midsummer feeding is a tolerate-and-watch call rather than a trigger for anything stronger. Lures work against you on a single planting by drawing beetles in from beyond it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put the shrub somewhere open where air actually moves through it, and keep it from growing into a solid thicket, so the leaves dry off after rain and dew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Site and canopy openness are the preventive half. An open position with real air movement, plus thinning that keeps the interior from closing in, shortens how long foliage stays wet. Set at planting where you have the choice.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This rust moves back and forth between elderberry and sedges, a group of grassy weeds, and it needs both to keep going. Pull the sedges growing near the planting and keep that ground clear, and you take away the other half of the cycle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungus is host-alternating between elderberry and nearby sedges, so clearing sedges from around the planting cuts the cycle at the point elderberry alone cannot supply. This is host removal rather than general tidiness, which is worth knowing before clearing ground that was doing no harm.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut off the shoots and clusters carrying the orange spots and the swollen, distorted growths as soon as you spot them, and take them out of the garden instead of dropping them under the bush.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt excision of infected shoots and flower clusters lowers what is producing spores inside the planting, and the material goes off site rather than under the shrub. This is removal of affected tissue and it works alongside the sedge clearing rather than in place of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune to open the bush up so air moves through the middle of it. This mildew gets going on crowded growth in still air late in summer, and an open plant is the main thing working against it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Opening the canopy is the lever that matters, since the fungus builds where growth is dense and air movement is poor, typically late in the season. An established shrub carries a fair amount of it without real harm, so the aim is keeping the plant open rather than chasing the film.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not over-feed the shrub. Heavy feeding gives you a thick flush of soft growth, which is exactly the crowded canopy this mildew does well in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen keeps the shrub from producing the dense, soft growth that closes the canopy and holds humidity in it. This is a feeding habit rather than a rescue, so it is set well before the white film shows up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the growth that is worst affected, and then leave it be. An established elderberry usually carries late-season mildew without real harm, so this is generally as far as you need to take it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing the badly affected growth is where the response stops on an established shrub, which usually tolerates the infection without treatment. Dulled late-season foliage is the typical cost, so escalating past this is hard to justify on a plant of this vigor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take the oldest canes out on a regular yearly schedule rather than letting them grow old and tired on the shrub, since these fungi get into old, stressed and winter-damaged wood. Carry what you cut well away from the bush instead of stacking it beside the planting.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scheduled renewal of old wood is the preventive half: these pathogens colonize old, stressed and winter-injured canes rather than sound young ones, so keeping the shrub on a renewal cycle limits how much susceptible wood is standing. Prunings leave the site rather than piling up next to the plant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where a cane carries a sunken, discolored patch, called a canker, cut the cane well below that patch and into wood that still looks healthy, then destroy the piece you removed. Wipe or dip your pruners between cuts. Try not to leave the shrub any fresh wounds you did not need to make, because wounds are how these fungi get in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Place the cut below the visible lesion margin into sound tissue and destroy what comes off; how far below you cut is what decides whether the excision holds. Disinfect between cuts, and keep needless wounding to a minimum while you work, since wounds and winter injury are the entry points these pathogens use.
